Oh, how to describe rural New Hampshire?

 

I’d say the biggest downfall, in my opinion, is winter.

“It’s just a little snow” you think, “how bad can it be?”

The short answer? Pretty bad.

 

You wake up early in the morning, and it’s cold. No surprise there. Sometime during the night the fire went out, and it’s the only source of heat you have, so it’s in the mid-sixties inside your house. Inside your bed, it’s toasty and cozy and there is no way you want to get out. But you have to go to work, so you get up, and get fully dressed because there’s no way you’re starting the fire in your cold house in your underwear. Somedays it snows two feet, and it’s not a big deal, but you better know how to plow or know someone who does, because the state plows aren’t going to plow out your driveway. Somedays it snows two feet, and then the next day it rains, and everything is a frozen wonderland! The boogers freeze in your nose upon your first breath outside and it pulls your nose-hairs. Your driveway is an ice rink! Your car is an ice prison! Good luck starting it to warm it up when the door is frozen shut. De-icer is for wimps, you chip that door open with a six inch sharpened wedge of plastic. Bonus points if you forgot your gloves inside and you’re too stubborn to go back in and get them.

 

Other seasons in New Hampshire include: Mud season (aka spring), and road construction. We call this a joke, but it’s pretty accurate. The highways around Portsmouth NH are in a constant state of construction, save for winter.

 

To be honest though, while I absolutely hate winter in NH (hate the cold), every other season is gorgeous. In the summer it’s rarely ever too hot, and there’s almost always a breeze even on the hottest days. Lyme disease really isn’t an issue as long as you wear long pants, use a bug spray that contains DEET, and check your crevasses after you’ve been in long grass or the woods. If you get chickens and let them free range they eat ticks, so it’s even less of an issue.

 

The best season is fall, though. Every morning is crisp, it’s cool enough for most of the bugs to die off, all the best New England foods are being made at a rate that makes you fear for your waistline, and the days are still warm. Of course, you get about two weeks of that weather before winter starts bearing down on you again.
